content.intro: Learn sql injection prevention through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: SQL Injection Prevention matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines sql injection prevention as part of security and privacy. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: ORM parameterization; Safe raw SQL; Avoiding dynamic SQL concatenation; Validating and limiting query inputs; Reviewing third-party database code. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: ORM parameterization
items.text: For ORM parameterization, identify the Django component responsible, the inputs and outputs it owns, and the boundary conditions that matter. Use the accompanying example as a starting point, verify it with the official versioned documentation, and record one test demonstrating expected behavior.

items.title: Safe raw SQL
items.text: Use parameterized SQL for dynamic values. Never concatenate untrusted input into SQL text; prefer the ORM for routine model queries and document backend-specific behavior when SQL is necessary.

items.title: Avoiding dynamic SQL concatenation
items.text: Avoiding dynamic SQL concatenation affects persistence and data correctness. Keep invariants in validation and database constraints where appropriate, inspect generated SQL/migrations, and test both expected data and error/rollback behavior.

items.title: Validating and limiting query inputs
items.text: Validating and limiting query inputs should be evaluated using a representative workload and a measured baseline. Compare correctness and resource usage before and after the change; the best choice depends on the database backend, request mix and data size.

items.title: Reviewing third-party database code
items.text: Reviewing third-party database code affects persistence and data correctness. Keep invariants in validation and database constraints where appropriate, inspect generated SQL/migrations, and test both expected data and error/rollback behavior.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First identify the input and the responsible Django component. Next trace how the example moves through “SQL Injection Prevention” and the related concept “ORM parameterization”. Predict the result before running or inspecting it. Finally compare the observed behavior with the expected result and the cited official documentation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or configuration choice related to ORM parameterization. Write down the expected outcome, test one normal case and one invalid or boundary case, then record what changed. Do not add real credentials or sensitive production data.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.
